body.text: Since 2017, over 1 million Rohingya refugees fled repression in Myanmar’s Rakhine State in waves to shelter at refugee camps and other places in Bangladesh. Some are now returning to Myanmar to villages from which they were displaced years ago.
Between February 10 and 15, The Diplomat interviewed members of two families at Maungdaw in Myanmar’s Rakhine State who undertook the perilous journey from Bangladesh to return home.

Rakhine State witnessed severe disturbances from the middle of 2024 when the Arakan Army (AA) intensified its campaign to wrest control over the area from the Myanmar military. The battles triggered displacement from villages inhabited by Rohingya Muslims, Rakhine Buddhists, and other communities.

Among those displaced from Maung Ni Para village at Maungdaw in Rakhine State was a Rohingya fisherman named Abdur Rahman, who crossed into Bangladesh after a long trek of seven hours with his family of seven members.

“My wife had to be carried all the way as she was in an advanced stage of pregnancy. We knew that Maungdaw would be extremely unsafe. There would be battles, bombings, and destruction of infrastructure,” said Rahman. “So, we decided to have the child delivered in Bangladesh.”

Rahman, his wife, four children, and sister-in-law began their trek to the border on June 29, 2024. They reached Teknaf in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar the following day. His son was born at a rented house there two months later. Subsequently, they moved to a refugee camp in Balukhali about 40 km north of Teknaf.

Rahman’s troubles worsened when all the money he had brought from home was exhausted in seven months. Two of his children were falling sick often, and he had to spend large sums on their diagnosis and medication. Meanwhile, he learnt that after the AA took control of Maungdaw it had established health centers with doctors.

However, his family was unable to firm up a plan to return to Rakhine State for another two months. “Many in the camp dissuaded us from returning home. We heard of some cases of camp inmates who were either killed or jailed by the military regime after they returned to Maungdaw. We were really confused for some time,” Rahman explained.

It was not until the beginning of April 2025 that the household finally resolved to return their home in Maungdaw. There were two routes to reach Maungdaw. The longer one was the land route they had taken to cross over into Bangladesh, but it was fraught with dangers and uncertainties. Rumors swirled in the refugee camp that Rohingya rebel groups such as the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) had a presence along the border. These groups were opposed to refugees returning to their homes in Maungdaw.

“Still, it was a risk worth taking as we were certain of a better life at our home in Maungdaw. Fortunately, we were able to connect with some fishermen who operated in the Naf River, and one of them agreed to ferry us across to Maungdaw,” recalled Rahman.

The journey home was easier than what Rahman’s family envisaged. In the late afternoon on April 24, 2025, all seven members of Rahman’s family quietly slipped out of the refugee camp and gathered at a spot 40 km away on the banks of the Naf River in Teknaf. A boatman who was paid in advance for the journey was waiting to transport them across the river.

“We reached Kyauk Hla Gar at around 10 pm on the other bank of the Naf in Maungdaw. We were relieved that nobody noticed us. Then we trekked for another 20 km to reach our home in Maung Ni Para village,” Rahman recalled.

Rahman’s house was intact, but all the household items had been stolen. It took the family another four months to settle down, using money they borrowed from relatives to buy essential goods. Meanwhile, Rahman returned to his work as a fisherman but has faced severe financial hardship.

Rahman claimed to know 38 other families from the refugee camps in Balukhali who had returned to Maungdaw earlier. Most of these families had escaped to Bangladesh during the AA-military battles in 2024, when the Myanmar military was engaging in forced conscription of Rohingya youths with the assistance of ARSA. Several families that had escaped to Bangladesh in 2017 during the military’s “clearance operations,” have also returned to Rakhine State.

According to Maung Ni Para village headman Noor Rashid, at least 100 returning refugees were imprisoned by the military on arriving at the village, and some of them fled back to Bangladesh after being released.

In 2017, the military burned down Padin village, as some youth from the village had been motivated by ARSA to carry out attacks on police outposts. Mohammad Rafiq left the village in mid-September with his family of six. After halting for a week at Pan Pyin Daw on the banks of the Naf River, “we crossed over to Teknaf in Bangladesh by boat, following on the trail of other residents of Maungdaw. After a week, we were brought to Leda Alihali camp by the police, where we stayed until December 7, 2018,” Rafiq said.

The camp was overcrowded and faced occasional food shortages. The inmates were often bullied and extorted by members of ARSA. The decision to return home was arrived at collectively by the family in mid-November of 2018.

On December 7, Rafiq and his family boarded a boat in Teknaf at 7:30 pm that took them across to Maungdaw. They reached the village three days later, only to find their house completely charred, with only a few half-burnt wooden poles.
Rafiq’s family stayed in tents for two months until a new thatched house was built. The family escaped being prosecuted as the military never received information about their return.

According to Rafiq, there were about 2,000 refugees who had relocated from Bangladesh to Maungdaw following the “clearance operations.” His claims could not be independently verified, but they were echoed by a senior functionary of AA’s political wing, the United League of Arakan, who was of the view that many Rohingya residents had returned and had settled in different locations in Rakhine State.

The ULA follows a lenient policy for returnees who fled during the battle in 2024 and a legal process for those who had escaped during the “clearance operations” in 2017. Refugees who were engaged with ARSA face harsher penalties, with jail terms ranging from 3 to 5 years.
